EN-1.t: Trace thyroid development from an endodermal diverticulum at the foramen cecum of the tongue, its descent along the thyroglossal duct anterior to the hyoid bone, and relate failed descent to a lingual thyroid.

Identify the pharyngeal pouch origins of the inferior parathyroids (third pouch, with the thymus), superior parathyroids (fourth pouch), and parafollicular C cells (ultimobranchial body, neural crest), and predict ectopic inferior parathyroid locations in the mediastinum.

Distinguish the origin of the anterior pituitary (Rathke pouch, oral ectoderm) from the posterior pituitary (infundibulum, diencephalic neuroectoderm), and relate Rathke pouch remnants to craniopharyngioma.
Compare the mesodermal origin of the adrenal cortex with the neural crest origin of the adrenal medulla, and relate the medulla's neural crest origin to pheochromocytoma and neuroblastoma.

Explain how failed development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches in 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge) syndrome produces neonatal hypocalcemic tetany together with thymic hypoplasia and T cell deficiency.
Describe development of the pancreatic islets from foregut endoderm of the dorsal and ventral pancreatic buds.

EN-2.t: Identify thyroid follicles (cuboidal follicular cells surrounding colloid) and parafollicular C cells, and relate tall columnar cells with scalloped, scant colloid to an actively stimulated gland, as in Graves disease.

Distinguish the zona glomerulosa, zona fasciculata, zona reticularis, and medulla of the adrenal gland by histology and principal product (aldosterone, cortisol, adrenal androgens, catecholamines from chromaffin cells).

Distinguish anterior pituitary acidophils (GH, prolactin), basophils (FSH, LH, ACTH, TSH), and chromophobes from the posterior pituitary, which contains pituicytes and Herring bodies formed by axon terminals of hypothalamic neurons.
Identify parathyroid chief cells (PTH secretion) and oxyphil cells, and identify pancreatic islet alpha, beta, and delta cells by their hormones (glucagon, insulin, somatostatin).

Classify endocrine cells by derivation (neural crest: chromaffin cells and C cells; endoderm: thyroid follicular cells, parathyroids, islets; ectoderm: adenohypophysis) and relate neuroendocrine origin to chromogranin and synaptophysin staining of neuroendocrine tumors.

EN-3.t: Locate the thyroid lobes and the isthmus anterior to the second and third tracheal rings, and explain why the gland, enclosed in pretracheal fascia, moves upward on swallowing.

Describe the relationship of the recurrent laryngeal nerve (tracheoesophageal groove) and external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (with the superior thyroid artery) to the thyroid, and predict voice changes after injury during thyroidectomy.

Locate the four parathyroid glands on the posterior surface of the thyroid lobes, and explain why their variable position, especially of the inferior glands, matters in thyroid and parathyroid surgery.

Locate the pituitary in the sella turcica beneath the diaphragma sellae, relate it to the optic chiasm above and cavernous sinuses laterally, and predict bitemporal hemianopia from suprasellar tumor extension.

Locate the retroperitoneal adrenal glands within the renal fascia superomedial to the kidneys, contrasting the pyramidal right gland behind the inferior vena cava with the crescent-shaped left gland along the medial border of the left kidney.

EN-4.t: Trace the thyroid's arterial supply (superior thyroid artery from the external carotid, inferior thyroid artery from the thyrocervical trunk, occasional thyroid ima artery) and venous drainage (superior and middle to internal jugular, inferior to brachiocephalic).

Trace the hypothalamo-hypophyseal portal system from superior hypophyseal arteries through the median eminence plexus and portal veins to the anterior pituitary, and explain why the anterior lobe is vulnerable to ischemic necrosis.

Trace the adrenal arteries (superior from inferior phrenic, middle from aorta, inferior from renal) and veins (right to inferior vena cava, left to left renal vein), and explain how cortical blood reaching the medulla induces PNMT for epinephrine synthesis.
Explain why the parathyroids depend mainly on the inferior thyroid artery, and predict hypocalcemia after thyroidectomy from devascularization or removal of parathyroid tissue.
Explain why insulin and glucagon draining into the hepatic portal vein reach the liver at high concentration first, and relate this to hepatic first-pass extraction of insulin.

EN-5.t: Match each hypothalamic hormone (TRH, CRH, GnRH, GHRH, somatostatin, dopamine) to its anterior pituitary target, and predict the effect of pituitary stalk section (rising prolactin, falling other anterior pituitary hormones, diabetes insipidus).

Explain control of ADH release by plasma osmolality (hypothalamic osmoreceptors) and blood volume (baroreceptors), and its action on V2 receptors inserting aquaporin-2 channels into collecting duct principal cells.

Explain calcium homeostasis: calcium-sensing receptor control of PTH, PTH effects on bone resorption, distal tubule calcium reabsorption, proximal tubule phosphate excretion, and renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase, and the opposing action of calcitonin.
EN-5.usmle: Multisystem: Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance disorders: hypocalcemia, hypercalcemia

EN-5.t: Explain regulation of aldosterone by angiotensin II and hyperkalemia (ACTH having a minor role), and its collecting duct actions: sodium reabsorption (ENaC, Na/K-ATPase) and potassium secretion by principal cells, and hydrogen ion secretion by alpha intercalated cells.

Trace glucose-stimulated insulin secretion (GLUT2 entry, glucokinase, rising ATP closing K-ATP channels, depolarization, calcium influx, exocytosis), and explain why oral glucose releases more insulin than intravenous glucose through incretins (GLP-1, GIP).
Explain glucose counterregulation during fasting and hypoglycemia, comparing the rapid effects of glucagon and epinephrine with the slower effects of cortisol and growth hormone.

EN-6.t: Classify hormones by signaling pathway: Gs/cAMP (ACTH, TSH, LH, FSH, PTH, glucagon), Gq/IP3-calcium (GnRH, TRH, oxytocin), intrinsic tyrosine kinase (insulin, IGF-1), JAK/STAT (GH, prolactin), and intracellular receptors (steroids, thyroid hormone, calcitriol).

Explain plasma transport of thyroid hormone (thyroxine-binding globulin) and cortisol (cortisol-binding globulin), why only free hormone is active, and predict raised total T4 with normal free T4 when binding globulin rises in pregnancy.

Interpret paired trophic and target hormone levels (for example, high cortisol with low ACTH, or low free T4 with high TSH) to localize an endocrine disorder to the target gland, pituitary, or hypothalamus by negative feedback logic.

Describe actions of thyroid hormone (raised basal metabolic rate and Na/K-ATPase, beta-1 adrenergic receptor upregulation, bone growth, CNS maturation) and its activation by peripheral deiodinase conversion of T4 to T3.

Explain direct GH actions (lipolysis, insulin antagonism) and indirect actions through hepatic IGF-1 (linear growth, protein synthesis), and GH regulation by GHRH, somatostatin, IGF-1 feedback, sleep, exercise, and hypoglycemia.

Explain cortisol's effects (gluconeogenesis, proteolysis, lipolysis, anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive actions, permissive effect on catecholamine vasoconstriction, reduced collagen synthesis) and the morning peak of ACTH and cortisol secretion.
Explain tonic dopamine inhibition of prolactin secretion and TRH stimulation of prolactin, and predict hypogonadism from hyperprolactinemia through suppression of GnRH.
EN-6.usmle: Endocrine: Pituitary disorders: Prolactinoma and hyperprolactinemia

EN-7.t: Contrast insulin's effects (GLUT4 uptake in muscle and adipose, glycogen synthesis, glycolysis, lipogenesis, protein synthesis) with glucagon's effects (glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, ketogenesis) on fuel metabolism in the fed and fasting states.

Explain how insulin deficiency with glucagon excess increases lipolysis, hepatic fatty acid oxidation, and conversion of acetyl-CoA to acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate, producing an anion gap metabolic acidosis.
EN-7.usmle: Endocrine: Diabetes mellitus: acute complications: ketoacidosis

EN-7.t: Relate dietary iodine to thyroid hormone synthesis and selenium to the deiodinases that convert T4 to T3, and explain how iodine deficiency raises TSH and causes goiter.

Trace vitamin D activation (UVB conversion of 7-dehydrocholesterol in skin, hepatic 25-hydroxylation, renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation stimulated by PTH and low phosphate) and predict rickets, osteomalacia, and secondary hyperparathyroidism from deficiency.
Explain how hypomagnesemia impairs PTH secretion and end-organ PTH action, producing hypocalcemia that does not correct until magnesium is replaced.
EN-7.usmle: Multisystem: Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance disorders: hypomagnesemia

EN-7.t: Explain how leptin from adipocytes (satiety) and ghrelin from the stomach (hunger) act on the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus to regulate appetite, and relate leptin resistance to common obesity and visceral adiposity to insulin resistance.

EN-8.t: Trace thyroid hormone synthesis: iodide uptake by the sodium-iodide symporter, oxidation and organification by thyroid peroxidase onto thyroglobulin tyrosines, coupling of MIT and DIT to T3 and T4, and release by thyroglobulin proteolysis.

Trace adrenal steroid synthesis from cholesterol (StAR transport, side-chain cleavage) through 17-alpha-hydroxylase, 21-hydroxylase, and 11-beta-hydroxylase to aldosterone, cortisol, and androgens, and predict which precursors accumulate when each enzyme is blocked.
EN-8.usmle: Endocrine: Congenital disorders: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia

EN-8.t: Trace catecholamine synthesis from tyrosine (tyrosine hydroxylase as rate-limiting step, DOPA decarboxylase, dopamine beta-hydroxylase, PNMT) and breakdown by COMT and MAO to metanephrines and vanillylmandelic acid, and relate these metabolites to pheochromocytoma testing.

Describe processing of preproinsulin to proinsulin and then insulin plus C-peptide, and use C-peptide to distinguish endogenous hyperinsulinism (insulinoma, sulfonylurea ingestion) from exogenous insulin as the cause of hypoglycemia.
EN-8.usmle: Endocrine: Hypoglycemia and islet cell disorders: Hypoglycemia (surreptitious insulin use)

EN-8.t: Describe synthesis of ADH and oxytocin in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei, their axonal transport bound to neurophysins, and storage and release from the posterior pituitary.

Explain how renal 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 inactivates cortisol to cortisone to protect mineralocorticoid receptors, and predict hypertension with hypokalemia when it is inhibited by licorice (glycyrrhetinic acid).
EN-8.usmle: Endocrine: Adrenal disorders: Hypertensive endocrine disease

EN-9.t: Contrast loss-of-function mutation of the MEN1 tumor suppressor gene (menin, with a second hit needed in tumor cells) with gain-of-function mutation of the RET proto-oncogene in MEN2, and explain the autosomal dominant inheritance of both syndromes.
Explain the autosomal recessive inheritance of congenital adrenal hyperplasia, with CYP21A2 (21-hydroxylase) mutations as the most common cause.
EN-9.usmle: Endocrine: Congenital disorders: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia

EN-9.t: Compare the genetics of type 1 diabetes (HLA-DR3 and DR4 association), type 2 diabetes (polygenic, with higher monozygotic twin concordance than type 1), and maturity-onset diabetes of the young (autosomal dominant glucokinase or HNF1A mutations).

Relate thyroid cancer types to their characteristic mutations: BRAF V600E and RET/PTC rearrangements in papillary carcinoma, RAS mutations and PAX8-PPARG fusion in follicular carcinoma, and RET mutations in medullary carcinoma.

Distinguish androgen insensitivity syndrome (X-linked androgen receptor defect, 46,XY, female external genitalia, testes, no uterus, high testosterone and LH) from 5-alpha-reductase deficiency (low DHT, ambiguous genitalia that virilize at puberty).
EN-9.usmle: Endocrine: Congenital disorders: Androgen insensitivity/resistance syndrome; Disorders of sexual differentiation

EN-9.t: Distinguish primary hypogonadism (for example, Klinefelter syndrome 47,XXY, with high LH and FSH) from secondary hypogonadism (for example, Kallmann syndrome, failed GnRH neuron migration with anosmia, with low LH and FSH).
EN-9.usmle: Endocrine: Pituitary disorders: Hypogonadism, primary and secondary

EN-9.t: Explain how steroid and thyroid hormones bind intracellular receptors that act as transcription factors at hormone response elements in DNA (the thyroid hormone receptor pairing with the retinoid X receptor), and relate this to their slower onset than peptide hormones.

EN-10.t: Explain Graves disease as a type II hypersensitivity in which thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins activate the TSH receptor, and predict transient neonatal thyrotoxicosis from transplacental IgG.

Describe the immune mechanisms of Hashimoto thyroiditis (T cell mediated follicular cell destruction, antibodies against thyroid peroxidase and thyroglobulin), relate these antibodies to diagnosis, and relate chronic lymphoid stimulation to risk of thyroid B cell lymphoma.
EN-10.usmle: Endocrine: Thyroid disorders: Thyroiditis, including Hashimoto

EN-10.t: Explain T cell mediated beta cell destruction (insulitis) in type 1 diabetes, the use of autoantibodies (GAD65, insulin, IA-2, ZnT8) as markers, and slowly progressive autoimmune diabetes in adults (type 1.5, LADA).
EN-10.usmle: Endocrine: Diabetes mellitus: Type 1 and type 1.5 diabetes mellitus

EN-10.t: Contrast autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1 (AIRE mutation, autosomal recessive: chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, Addison disease) with type 2 (Addison disease with autoimmune thyroid disease or type 1 diabetes).
EN-10.usmle: Multisystem: Immunologic and inflammatory disorders: polyglandular autoimmune syndrome, type 1

EN-10.t: Explain how inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-alpha) activate the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, and how cortisol limits inflammation by inhibiting phospholipase A2 and NF-kB and reducing lymphocyte and eosinophil counts.

Explain why conjugating meningococcal capsular polysaccharide to a protein carrier turns a T cell independent response into a T cell dependent response with class switching and memory, and relate vaccination to prevention of Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome.

EN-11.t: Describe Neisseria meningitidis (gram-negative diplococcus, polysaccharide capsule, lipooligosaccharide endotoxin, respiratory droplet spread) and explain how endotoxin-driven sepsis and DIC cause adrenal hemorrhage in Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome.

Identify bacteria that cause acute suppurative thyroiditis (Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus pneumoniae), and relate recurrent left-sided infection in children to a pyriform sinus fistula.
Relate subacute granulomatous thyroiditis to a preceding viral upper respiratory infection, with viruses such as coxsackievirus and mumps implicated.

Identify infectious causes of adrenalitis leading to Addison disease, including Mycobacterium tuberculosis (acid-fast, caseating granulomas), Histoplasma capsulatum, and cytomegalovirus in patients with AIDS.

EN-12-A.t: Distinguish ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome (pituitary adenoma, ectopic ACTH from small cell lung carcinoma) from ACTH-independent causes (adrenal adenoma or carcinoma, exogenous glucocorticoids) using plasma ACTH and high-dose dexamethasone suppression.

Relate cortisol excess to central obesity, moon facies, purple striae, proximal muscle weakness, hyperglycemia, hypertension, osteoporosis, and poor wound healing, and identify screening tests (24-hour urine free cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol, low-dose dexamethasone suppression).

Explain primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome from adrenal adenoma, or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia) as hypertension with hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, and low renin, and contrast it with secondary hyperaldosteronism with high renin.

Predict findings in 21-hydroxylase deficiency (salt wasting, hyperkalemia, raised 17-hydroxyprogesterone, virilization), 11-beta-hydroxylase deficiency (virilization with hypertension), and 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency (hypertension, hypokalemia, absent sex steroids).
EN-12-A.usmle: Endocrine: Congenital disorders: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia

EN-12-A.t: Explain primary hyperparathyroidism, most often from a single parathyroid adenoma, and interpret hypercalcemia, hypophosphatemia, and raised PTH with stones, bone pain, abdominal symptoms, and osteitis fibrosa cystica (subperiosteal resorption, brown tumors).

Explain secondary hyperparathyroidism in chronic kidney disease (phosphate retention, low calcitriol) and vitamin D deficiency, interpret low or normal calcium with high PTH, and relate it to renal osteodystrophy and tertiary hyperparathyroidism.
EN-12-A.usmle: Endocrine: Parathyroid disorders: Metabolic bone disease

EN-12-A.t: Distinguish gigantism (GH excess before epiphyseal closure) from acromegaly (after closure), and relate acromegaly to coarse facial features, enlarged hands and feet, macroglossia, insulin resistance, and cardiovascular disease.
Interpret raised IGF-1 and failure of GH suppression after an oral glucose load as confirmation of GH excess, usually from a somatotroph pituitary adenoma.

Distinguish Graves disease (diffuse goiter, ophthalmopathy, pretibial myxedema, diffusely increased radioiodine uptake) from toxic multinodular goiter (patchy uptake, no eye or skin signs), both showing low TSH and high free T4.

Relate thyrotoxic findings (weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, tachycardia, atrial fibrillation, bone loss) to raised metabolic rate and beta-adrenergic sensitivity, and identify thyroid storm as a life-threatening complication.
EN-12-A.usmle: Endocrine: Thyroid disorders: Hyperthyroidism, thyrotoxicosis, thyroid storm

EN-12-A.t: Explain the syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (small cell lung carcinoma, CNS and pulmonary disease, drugs) and interpret euvolemic hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine and high urine sodium.
Distinguish familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (inactivating calcium-sensing receptor mutation, low urine calcium, mildly raised PTH) from primary hyperparathyroidism.

Distinguish central precocious puberty (early GnRH activation, raised LH and FSH) from peripheral precocious puberty (low LH and FSH, for example from congenital adrenal hyperplasia, McCune-Albright syndrome, or sex steroid secreting tumors).
EN-12-A.usmle: Endocrine: Adrenal disorders: Delayed and precocious puberty

EN-12-B.t: Distinguish central diabetes insipidus (ADH deficiency from head trauma, surgery, or tumors) from nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (V2 receptor or aquaporin-2 defects, lithium, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia), both causing polyuria with dilute urine and a tendency to hypernatremia when water intake is limited.
Interpret a water deprivation test with desmopressin, predicting urine concentration in central diabetes insipidus, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, and primary polydipsia.

Explain primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease; autoimmune adrenalitis, tuberculosis, metastases) and relate hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and hyperpigmentation from raised ACTH and POMC-derived MSH to low cortisol and aldosterone.
EN-12-B.usmle: Endocrine: Adrenal disorders: Corticoadrenal insufficiency (Addison disease)

EN-12-B.t: Identify causes of acute adrenocortical insufficiency (adrenal crisis), including stress in a patient with chronic insufficiency, rapid withdrawal of long-term glucocorticoids, and bilateral adrenal hemorrhage (anticoagulation, DIC, Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome), and relate it to shock.

Explain secondary adrenocortical insufficiency (pituitary disease, suppression by exogenous glucocorticoids) and predict why it lacks hyperpigmentation and hyperkalemia because ACTH is low and the renin-angiotensin system preserves aldosterone.
EN-12-B.usmle: Endocrine: Adrenal disorders: Adrenal insufficiency, secondary

EN-12-B.t: Identify causes of hypoparathyroidism (surgical removal, autoimmune, DiGeorge syndrome, hypomagnesemia) and relate hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and low PTH to tetany, perioral numbness, Chvostek and Trousseau signs, and QT prolongation.

Distinguish pseudohypoparathyroidism (end-organ PTH resistance from GNAS mutation, high PTH, Albright hereditary osteodystrophy with short fourth and fifth metacarpals) from true hypoparathyroidism with low PTH.

Identify causes of hypopituitarism (nonfunctioning macroadenoma, Sheehan necrosis, pituitary apoplexy, surgery or radiation), and explain primary empty sella syndrome as arachnoid herniation through a defective diaphragma sellae flattening the pituitary.

Predict findings of hypothalamic lesions (craniopharyngioma, infiltrative disease, radiation), including deficiency of releasing hormones with low anterior pituitary output, diabetes insipidus, and hyperprolactinemia from interrupted dopamine delivery.

Explain how iodine deficiency lowers thyroid hormone, raises TSH, and causes diffuse then multinodular goiter, and relate hypothyroidism to cold intolerance, weight gain, bradycardia, myxedema, hyperlipidemia, and delayed reflex relaxation.

Interpret thyroid function tests in primary hypothyroidism (high TSH, low free T4), central hypothyroidism (low or normal TSH, low free T4), and TSH-secreting adenoma (high TSH, high free T4), and relate hypothyroid hyperprolactinemia to menstrual disturbance and infertility.
EN-12-B.usmle: Endocrine: Thyroid disorders: Secondary hypothyroidism and hyperthyroidism

EN-12-B.t: Identify causes of congenital hypothyroidism (thyroid dysgenesis, dyshormonogenesis, maternal iodine deficiency) and relate them to lethargy, prolonged jaundice, macroglossia, umbilical hernia, and intellectual disability if untreated.
Interpret nonthyroidal illness (euthyroid sick) syndrome in severe illness, with low T3, raised reverse T3, and usually normal TSH from reduced peripheral T4 to T3 conversion.
EN-12-B.usmle: Endocrine: Thyroid disorders: Nonthyroidal illness syndrome (euthyroid sick syndrome)

EN-12-B.t: Distinguish causes of short stature, including GH deficiency (low IGF-1, delayed bone age), GH receptor defects (Laron syndrome, high GH, low IGF-1), constitutional growth delay (delayed bone age), and familial short stature (normal bone age).
EN-12-B.usmle: Endocrine: Pituitary disorders: Growth hormone deficiency; Short stature

EN-12-C.t: Explain the pathogenesis of Hashimoto thyroiditis and identify its histology (lymphocytic infiltrate with germinal centers, atrophic follicles, Hürthle cells) and painless goiter in a middle-aged woman.
EN-12-C.usmle: Endocrine: Thyroid disorders: Thyroiditis, including Hashimoto

EN-12-C.t: Predict the course of Hashimoto thyroiditis from possible transient hyperthyroidism to permanent hypothyroidism, its association with other autoimmune diseases, and its increased risk of primary thyroid B cell lymphoma.
EN-12-C.usmle: Endocrine: Thyroid disorders: Thyroiditis, including Hashimoto

EN-12-C.t: Identify granulomatous subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis by a painful, tender thyroid after a viral illness, fever, raised ESR, and granulomas with multinucleated giant cells, and predict transient hyperthyroidism with low radioiodine uptake.
Predict the self-limited course of subacute thyroiditis from a thyrotoxic phase to a transient hypothyroid phase and usual recovery to normal thyroid function.

Distinguish painless (lymphocytic and postpartum) thyroiditis and Riedel thyroiditis (IgG4-related dense fibrosis producing a rock-hard thyroid fixed to adjacent structures) from Hashimoto and subacute thyroiditis.

EN-12-D.t: Compare type 1 diabetes (autoimmune beta cell loss, absolute insulin deficiency, young onset, ketosis prone) with type 2 diabetes (insulin resistance with progressive beta cell dysfunction and islet amyloid, linked to obesity and family history).
EN-12-D.usmle: Endocrine: Diabetes mellitus: Type 1 diabetes mellitus; Type 2 diabetes mellitus

EN-12-D.t: Interpret diagnostic criteria for diabetes (fasting glucose at least 126 mg/dL, 2-hour oral glucose tolerance value at least 200 mg/dL, HbA1c at least 6.5%, or random glucose at least 200 mg/dL with symptoms) and explain HbA1c as a three-month measure.

Contrast diabetic ketoacidosis (anion gap acidosis, ketones, Kussmaul breathing, raised serum potassium despite total body depletion) with hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (very high glucose and osmolality, altered mental status, little ketosis).

Explain how nonenzymatic glycation (advanced glycation end products) and the sorbitol (polyol) pathway produce hyaline arteriolosclerosis, accelerated atherosclerosis, peripheral neuropathy, and cataracts in chronic hyperglycemia.

Predict chronic diabetic complications by organ: nephropathy (glomerular basement membrane thickening, Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules, albuminuria), retinopathy, autonomic neuropathy with gastroparesis, and peripheral vascular disease with foot ulcers.

Identify components of metabolic syndrome (abdominal obesity, high triglycerides, low HDL cholesterol, hypertension, raised fasting glucose), relate them to insulin resistance, and recognize acanthosis nigricans as a skin sign of insulin resistance.

EN-12-E.t: Explain how a persistent thyroglossal duct forms a midline neck cyst near the hyoid bone that moves upward with swallowing and tongue protrusion, and identify infection as a complication.

Distinguish a midline thyroglossal duct cyst from a lateral branchial cleft cyst at the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid, and explain why a normally located thyroid should be confirmed before removal, since the mass may be the only functioning thyroid tissue.

EN-12-F.t: Explain Sheehan syndrome as ischemic necrosis of a pregnancy-enlarged anterior pituitary after severe postpartum hemorrhage and hypotension, and explain why the posterior pituitary, with its direct arterial supply, is usually spared.
EN-12-F.usmle: Endocrine: Pituitary disorders: Pituitary apoplexy (Sheehan syndrome)

EN-12-F.t: Predict the presentation of Sheehan syndrome (failure of lactation, amenorrhea, loss of axillary and pubic hair, hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency) from loss of anterior pituitary hormones.

Explain pituitary apoplexy as sudden hemorrhage or infarction of a pituitary adenoma, and relate severe headache, visual loss, ophthalmoplegia from cavernous sinus compression, and acute adrenal insufficiency to its mechanism.

EN-12-G.t: Distinguish adrenal cortical adenoma (small, often nonfunctional or cortisol or aldosterone secreting) from adrenocortical carcinoma (large, invasive, often virilizing), and recognize that metastases are more common than primary adrenal cancer.
EN-12-G.usmle: Endocrine: Adrenal disorders: Neoplasms (adrenal carcinoma, adrenal adenoma, aldosteronoma, incidentaloma)

EN-12-G.t: Identify neuroblastoma as an adrenal medulla tumor of young children with N-MYC amplification, Homer Wright rosettes, raised urine homovanillic acid and vanillylmandelic acid, and possible opsoclonus-myoclonus.
Identify insulinoma as a beta cell tumor causing Whipple triad (hypoglycemic symptoms, low glucose, relief with glucose) with inappropriately high insulin and C-peptide, and relate it to MEN1.
EN-12-G.usmle: Endocrine: Hypoglycemia and islet cell disorders: Islet cell tumors, insulinoma

EN-12-G.t: Distinguish causes of hypoglycemia, including insulinoma (high insulin and C-peptide), surreptitious insulin use (high insulin, low C-peptide), sepsis, and liver failure (impaired gluconeogenesis and glycogen stores).
EN-12-G.usmle: Endocrine: Hypoglycemia and islet cell disorders: Hypoglycemia

EN-12-G.t: Identify other pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors by their syndromes: glucagonoma (hyperglycemia, necrolytic migratory erythema, weight loss) and somatostatinoma (diabetes, gallstones, steatorrhea, achlorhydria).
EN-12-G.usmle: Endocrine: Hypoglycemia and islet cell disorders: Hyperglycemia secondary to glucagonoma; somatostatinoma; Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors

EN-12-G.t: Distinguish parathyroid adenoma (single enlarged gland of chief cells, suppressed remaining glands), hyperplasia (multiple glands, as in MEN syndromes), and the rare carcinoma (marked hypercalcemia, invasion, metastasis).

Classify pituitary adenomas by size (microadenoma under 1 cm, macroadenoma) and hormone, and relate prolactinoma, the most common type, to galactorrhea, amenorrhea, and infertility in women and decreased libido in men.
EN-12-G.usmle: Endocrine: Pituitary disorders: Neoplasms; Prolactinoma and hyperprolactinemia; Galactorrhea

EN-12-G.t: Predict mass effects of a nonfunctioning pituitary macroadenoma: bitemporal hemianopia from chiasm compression, headache, hypopituitarism, and mild hyperprolactinemia from stalk compression.

Identify craniopharyngioma as a suprasellar tumor from Rathke pouch remnants, often calcified and cystic with oily fluid, causing headache, bitemporal hemianopia, diabetes insipidus, and growth failure in children.
Distinguish follicular adenoma from follicular carcinoma by capsular or vascular invasion, and explain hematogenous spread of follicular carcinoma to bone and lung.

Identify papillary carcinoma, the most common thyroid cancer, by Orphan Annie eye nuclei, nuclear grooves, and psammoma bodies, relate it to childhood radiation exposure, and explain lymphatic spread to cervical nodes with good prognosis.
Identify medullary carcinoma as a C cell tumor secreting calcitonin, with amyloid stroma derived from calcitonin, and relate it to RET mutations and MEN2.

Distinguish euthyroid (nontoxic) diffuse and multinodular goiter, with normal TSH and compressive symptoms such as dysphagia, from thyroid neoplasms, and relate a cold nodule on radioiodine scan to higher cancer risk.
EN-12-G.usmle: Endocrine: Thyroid disorders: Goiter; Cyst, nodule

EN-12-G.t: Identify anaplastic thyroid carcinoma as a rapidly growing, locally invasive tumor of older adults with TP53 mutations and very poor prognosis.

Match the tumors of MEN1 (parathyroid, pituitary, pancreatic endocrine tumors such as gastrinoma), MEN2A (medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, parathyroid hyperplasia), and MEN2B (medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas, marfanoid habitus).

Identify pheochromocytoma as a chromaffin cell tumor causing episodic hypertension, headache, palpitations, and sweating, diagnosed by raised plasma or urine metanephrines, and associated with MEN2, von Hippel-Lindau disease, and neurofibromatosis type 1.

Identify endocrine paraneoplastic syndromes: ACTH and ADH from small cell lung carcinoma, and hypercalcemia of malignancy from PTH-related peptide (squamous cell lung carcinoma, renal cell carcinoma) with suppressed PTH.

EN-12-H.t: Identify acute infectious (suppurative) thyroiditis as a bacterial infection presenting with fever and a painful, tender, sometimes fluctuant thyroid with usually normal thyroid function, and identify abscess as a complication.

Explain Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome as bilateral adrenal hemorrhage during overwhelming sepsis, classically meningococcemia with DIC, and relate petechial rash, shock, and acute adrenal insufficiency to its mechanism.
